Cautiously positive. The FOMC characterizes growth as “solid,” notes further disinflation, and delivers a 50 bp rate cut—signals that are dovish but framed by “balanced” risks and continued balance-sheet runoff. In the literature, this mix aligns with flexible inflation targeting and inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson 1997a; Svensson and Woodford 1999): easing is justified when projected inflation is near target, reducing the central bank’s loss function. Data dependence and “balanced risks” mirror Taylor-rule guidance and Phillips-curve stabilization, aiming to support the output gap (IS curve) without reigniting inflation. Continuing QT helps preserve credibility against time-inconsistency and inflation-bias concerns (Barro-Gordon; Rogoff’s conservative central banker). With inflation expectations kept near a 2% anchor, the welfare costs of inflation (e.g., Dotsey; Ireland) fall—a positive. Offsetting this, slower job gains, a higher unemployment rate, and explicit uncertainty temper the tone. Net assessment: mildly positive/dovish.
